## Why? {#why}

**Research question:** Do drivers respond faster to haptic takeover warnings than to visual ones, and do they get faster over the trials?

In the driving simulator (`driving_sim`), each of the 40 participants drives 12 takeovers: 3 modalities × 4 trials. The 12 measurements of one person are related; some people are generally faster. The repeated-measures ANOVA (lesson Group comparisons) averages per person and condition for this and so loses the trial and every person with a missing value. A **mixed model** uses all single measurements and represents the dependence through random effects.

## Concept {#concept}

```{=html}

<figcaption>On the left, each person may have their own baseline but learns equally fast. On the right, the practice effect may also vary between people. The middle line is the fixed effect you report.</figcaption>

```

- **Formula** `lmer(y ~ fixed effects + (random effects | group))`: fixed effects are what you want to test (modality, trial). In brackets is what may vary per group: `(1 | participant)` a baseline of its own per person.
- **Tests:** lme4 gives no p-values. With **lmerTest** loaded, `summary()` and `anova()` provide tests with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; `parameters::model_parameters()` shows CIs.
- **Random slope** `(1 + trial_c | participant)`: the effect may also vary between people. Rule of thumb: effects that vary *within* the person and can differ between people get a random slope, otherwise the tests are too liberal. Person characteristics (`experience`) never do.
- **ICC** `performance::icc(fit)`: share of the variance between groups. High means: further trials of the same person bring little new information.
- **Crossed or nested:** if all participants work on the same tasks, participant and task are crossed: `(1 | participant) + (1 | task)`. Nested (`(1 | school/class)`) means each class belongs to exactly one school.
- **Singular:** "boundary (singular) fit" means a variance is ≈ 0 or a correlation ≈ ±1. Then simplify the random structure step by step and report it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## More: REML, model comparison, effect sizes

- **REML vs. ML:** `lmer()` estimates with REML by default (unbiased variances). For model comparisons with different *fixed* effects, `anova(m1, m2)` needs ML; it refits automatically for this (`refit = TRUE`). For different random structures with the same fixed effects use `anova(m1, m2, refit = FALSE)`.
- **R² for mixed models:** `performance::r2(fit)` gives the marginal R² (fixed effects only, here 0.24) and the conditional one (with random effects, 0.65).
- **Contrasts and means** work as with afex: `modelbased::estimate_contrasts(fit, contrast = "condition", p_adjust = "holm")` or emmeans.
- **Convergence warnings:** `lme4::allFit(fit)` refits with all optimisers; if the estimates agree, the warning is usually harmless.
:::

## Example {#example}

Modality with a random intercept per person, and for comparison an `lm()` that ignores the dependence:

```{webr}
fit <- lmer(rt_ms ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = driving_sim)
model_parameters(fit)
model_parameters(lm(rt_ms ~ condition, data = driving_sim))
```

The estimates are almost the same (auditory −159 vs. −161 ms), the standard errors are not: the mixed model estimates the modality effects *within* participants (SE 13.3 instead of 19.7 ms), because it removes the differences between people from the error. How much is that?

```{webr}
icc(lmer(rt_ms ~ 1 + (1 | participant), data = driving_sim))
anova(fit)
```

ICC = 0.40: 40% of the variance lies between participants. Modality: F(2, 426) = 157.6, p < .001.

**How to report it:** A linear mixed model with a random intercept per participant (ICC of the null model = .40) showed an effect of warning modality, F(2, 426) = 157.6, p < .001 (Satterthwaite). Compared with visual warnings, participants responded 159 ms faster to auditory ones, 95% CI [133, 185], and 231 ms faster to haptic ones [205, 258].

## Package comparison {#packages}

| Task | Recommendation | Alternative |
|---|---|---|
| Linear mixed model | **lme4** `lmer()` + **lmerTest** (Satterthwaite) | `afex::mixed()` (type III tests, Kenward-Roger); nlme `lme()` (correlation structures over time) |
| Non-normal data | `lme4::glmer()` (binomial, poisson) | **glmmTMB** (negative binomial, zero inflation, beta), locally |
| Results, variance shares | **parameters** `model_parameters()`, **performance** `icc()`, `r2()`, `check_model()` | `summary()`, `VarCorr()`, `broom.mixed::tidy()` |
| Bayesian | – | brms (Stan), locally |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Run locally: glmmTMB

glmmTMB currently does not load in the browser (version conflict with TMB in the webR package index). Locally: error counts per task with overdispersion as a negative binomial model.

```r
library(glmmTMB)
fit_nb <- glmmTMB(errors ~ prototype + (1 | participant) + (1 | task),
                  family = nbinom2, data = usability)
model_parameters(fit_nb, exponentiate = TRUE)
```
:::

## Cheat sheet {#cheatsheet}

```r
library(lmerTest)   # lmer() with Satterthwaite tests

# Random intercept per person
fit <- lmer(rt_ms ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = d)
anova(fit)                    # type III, Satterthwaite
model_parameters(fit)         # estimates, CIs, random effects

# Random slope, trial centred
d <- d |> mutate(trial_c = trial - 2.5)
fit_rs <- lmer(rt_ms ~ condition + trial_c + (1 + trial_c | participant), data = d)
coef(fit_rs)$participant      # slope per person (fixed + deviation)
isSingular(fit_rs); VarCorr(fit_rs)

# Crossed: participant × task
fit_x <- lmer(log(time_s) ~ prototype + (1 | participant) + (1 | task), data = u)
icc(fit_x, by_group = TRUE); r2(fit_x)

# Residuals row by row with missing values
fit <- lmer(rt_ms ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = d, na.action = na.exclude)
```
